title: Donald Trump announces 1776 Commission to end black history in schools

description_long:
Donald Trump announced an executive order creating the 1776 Commission on September 17, 2020. He presented it as an effort to promote “patriotic” history in schools and criticized the New York Times’ 1619 Project and critical race theory, which he said distorted the country’s history. His remarks came amid public disputes over how schools teach slavery, racism, and the nation’s past.

The proposed commission was a federal intervention in that debate, framed by Trump as a response to what he portrayed as an overly negative account of American history. The announcement drew criticism, including from commentator Ana Kasparian, who objected to the implication that students should learn less about racism and slavery. The action documented here is the executive order and Trump’s stated rationale. The announcement alone does not show that a particular school changed its instruction. title: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_short: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_medium: A bipartisan Senate report released in June 2022 found that Capitol Police received at least 14 specific warnings of possible violence before the January 6, 2021 attack. It described failures to act on intelligence across law-enforcement agencies and noted that Trump advisers had received threat briefings. Donald Trump himself received no intelligence briefing that morning because he had not requested one.
description_long:
A bipartisan Senate report released on June 7, 2022, examined intelligence and security preparations for the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. It found that the Capitol Police had received at least 14 specific warnings about possible violence but did not adequately prepare. The report described a wider failure among law-enforcement agencies to coordinate and act on intelligence. It also said senior executive-branch officials, including advisers to President Donald Trump, had been briefed on threats without a corresponding increase in security.

Trump did not receive an intelligence briefing on the morning of January 6 because he had not requested one, according to testimony cited in the account. That distinguishes what his advisers knew from what was briefed directly to him. The Senate findings later informed the House January 6 Committee’s assessment of Trump’s inaction. The report documented warnings, briefing patterns, and security failures; it did not determine individual criminal liability. Its findings show that specific warnings existed before the attack and that agencies failed to respond adequately.

title: DOJ Sues 31 States for Voter Rolls While Threatening Officials with Arrest
description_short: DOJ Sues 31 States for Voter Rolls While Threatening Officials with Arrest
description_medium: The Justice Department sued election officials in 31 states seeking voter-registration data. Other reports described threats of funding cuts or arrest for officials who resisted removing names flagged by federal citizenship databases, including SAVE. Tens of thousands of registrations were reportedly flagged, including records belonging to U.S. citizens. The scope and chronology of those enforcement claims remain disputed.
description_long: By April 2026, internal DOJ communications obtained by CNN revealed the Trump administration had been working for nearly a year on a covert plan to use DHS's SAVE citizenship database to identify and remove noncitizens from voter rolls, while hiding the plan's details from courts and Democratic election officials. The DOJ had brought lawsuits against the election chiefs of 31 states — primarily Democratic — demanding unredacted voter registration data including Social Security numbers, arguing noncompliance violated federal law. By July 2026, AP News reported the administration was threatening to withhold federal funding from states and warning state election officials they faced arrest if they did not remove voters flagged by the federal system — despite multiple courts having rejected the efforts as based on 'untrue claims about widespread voting fraud.' At least 67 million voter registrations had been run through federal databases with tens of thousands flagged, including documented cases of U.S. citizens wrongly identified by the SAVE system.

title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_short: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_medium: Federal prosecutors indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James on bank-fraud and false-statement charges in October 2025 following a mortgage investigation. The account says U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert was removed after declining to bring charges, and a judge later dismissed the indictment because prosecutor Lindsey Halligan’s appointment was unlawful. Grand juries declined to re-indict James. The proceedings drew political-retaliation claims.
description_long: Letitia James, the New York Attorney General who had won a landmark $454 million civil fraud judgment against Trump and his companies in 2022, became a primary target of DOJ retaliation in Trump's second term. In March 2025, FHFA Director Bill Pulte — a Trump ally — referred James to the DOJ alleging she had misrepresented information on a mortgage application. Despite a five-month investigation finding insufficient evidence to indict, Trump fired U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert in September 2025 specifically for refusing to bring charges against James and Comey. Ed Martin, Trump's special attorney and Weaponization Working Group director, sent James's attorney a letter saying he would take her resignation as an act of good faith even before any charges were filed. In October 2025, Lindsey Halligan — the same unlawfully appointed prosecutor who indicted Comey — secured a grand jury indictment against James on charges of bank fraud and making false statements. James pleaded not guilty and called the charges baseless and driven by political retribution. On November 24, 2025, the same judge who dismissed the Comey case dismissed James's indictment on the same grounds: Halligan's unlawful appointment. Subsequent federal grand juries in both Norfolk and Alexandria declined to re-indict James. The DOJ appealed. The mortgage fraud investigations of both James and Schiff were themselves investigated for potential DOJ misconduct.

title: Trump-Endorsed Candidates Fail Across Midterms, Sparking GOP Civil War
description_short: Trump-Endorsed Candidates Fail Across Midterms, Sparking GOP Civil War
description_medium: The 2022 midterms did not produce the Republican “red wave” many expected, and several Trump-endorsed candidates who denied the 2020 election results lost high-profile races. Mehmet Oz, Blake Masters, Herschel Walker, and Doug Mastriano were among the defeated candidates. Ron DeSantis won reelection in Florida by 19 points. Republican leaders including Mitch McConnell publicly blamed Trump, intensifying debate over his influence in the party.
description_long:
In the November 2022 midterm elections, the anticipated Republican “red wave” failed to materialize. Several candidates endorsed by Donald Trump, including Mehmet Oz in Pennsylvania, Blake Masters in Arizona, Herschel Walker in Georgia, and Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate Doug Mastriano, lost their races. Meanwhile, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis won reelection by 19 points, giving him a prominent victory as Trump-backed candidates struggled elsewhere.

After the results, Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and other party figures publicly criticized Trump and his candidate choices. Their comments reflected an open dispute over whether the party should continue following Trump’s direction or move toward other leaders. The results accelerated calls among some Republicans for a post-Trump strategy, though they did not end Trump’s influence over the party. Some polling after the election found Trump especially unpopular among independent voters. The election outcomes and immediate party reaction intensified a debate over Trump’s place in the party; it does not claim that every endorsed candidate lost or that one election settled the Republican Party’s future. The contrast between DeSantis’s strong Florida result and several Trump-backed losses became part of the debate over who could lead the party next.

Former acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller said that in a January 5, 2021 meeting with Donald Trump, he and Kash Patel were discussing an Iran issue when Trump shifted to the January 6 demonstration. Miller recalled Trump saying, “You’re going to need 10,000 people.” Miller replied that National Guard support would be provided if requested by the District.
